title: Keep your footing
hookLine: turn outward to please someone and you've lost your footing (Enchiridion 23)

cards: You're in a meeting and your manager floats an idea you think won't work. You open your mouth to say so. Then you see their face, hopeful, a little proud, and you hear yourself say: yeah, that could be great.
Or you're at a party, someone makes a joke about a group of people, and you laugh along, a beat late, because everyone else did. Afterward there's a small wobble, as if the floor had tilted.
Section twenty-three of the handbook is only a few lines long, and it names that wobble exactly.

teach.b: If it ever happens, Epictetus says, that you turn outward because you want to please someone, know that you've lost your footing.
The Greek word is enstasis: a stance, a way of standing, a plan of life you've set yourself in. The moment you face outward to win approval, you've stepped off it. Kindness isn't the problem.
Bringing a friend soup, choosing the restaurant your partner likes, laughing at a child's bad joke: those can all come from your own footing.

The trouble is when the aim shifts from doing right to being liked, and you start bending your words to someone else's face. The remedy: be content, he says, in everything, simply to be a philosopher.
And if you also want to seem one, seem one to yourself. That's enough. It's a strangely freeing sentence.
You need one witness, and you already have them. Keeping your footing doesn't mean saying every harsh thing you think. In the meeting, it might sound like: I'm not sure that will work, can I say why?
At the party, it might be not laughing, and changing the subject.
Quiet, small, honest. People-pleasing can look like it buys peace. Epictetus thinks the price is higher than it looks.
Each tilt toward someone's approval hands them a little of the ground you stand on.

how: Some Stoic practitioners notice when they are shaping their words to win someone's approval, and return to saying what they actually think, kindly.

o: a stubborn refusal to ever change your mind
a stance: the plan of life you stand in
a polite habit of agreeing to keep peace

games.q: keep your footing — tap the pairs.
p: your stance, your plan of life
can come from your own footing

s: Epictetus says never do anything nice for anyone
kindness is fine; the trouble is bending your aim toward being liked.
he says if you want to seem a philosopher, seem one to yourself
section twenty-three is a long chapter
it's only a few lines long.

games.q: your manager's idea won't work, and they look hopeful. what keeps your footing?
o: say it's great so they're happy.
say, kindly, that you're not sure, and why.
games.why: turning outward to please, Epictetus says, means you've lost your stance. an honest, kind sentence keeps it.

practice: Plant your feet flat on the floor, standing or sitting, and feel your weight even on both.
Bring to mind a person you tend to bend toward, a boss, a parent, a friend whose approval you want, and notice whether your body leans, even slightly.
Come back to center, and picture saying one honest, kind sentence to them from right here.

wordCard.voice: Enstasis. The Greek word for your stance, the plan of life you've set yourself in; turn outward to please someone and you've stepped off it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 23: a stance, a footing, a plan of life.

carryVoice: Your line: keep my footing. Kind and honest can stand in the same place. Day three hundred fifty-five, done.
